title: Functional Fixedness
description: Getting stuck seeing objects or ideas only in their usual function, which blocks creative problem‑solving. You can’t see that a paperclip could also be a lock‑pick.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: Getting stuck seeing objects or ideas only in their usual function, which blocks creative problem‑solving. You can’t see that a paperclip could also be a lock‑pick.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A mechanic trying to open a stuck part doesn’t think to use a coin, only a wrench.
In a brainstorming session, the team only imagines the product in its current market, missing adjacent opportunities.
In a survival situation, people fail to use their phone’s screen as a signal mirror because they see it as “just a phone.”

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Repeating the same tool‑use patterns even when ineffective.
Rejecting unconventional solutions because “that’s not what it’s for.”
Staring at a problem with all the necessary items nearby but failing to combine them.

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You’re stuck and you’ve stopped scanning your environment for alternative resources.
You dismiss ideas because they break convention.
You think you need to buy or acquire something new when the solution is already in front of you.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: The brain organizes knowledge into schemas with fixed associations. This cognitive efficiency comes at the cost of flexibility: the primary association blinds you to secondary uses.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: When stuck, list every object around you and ask, “What else could this do?”
Deliberately consider “wrong” or absurd uses; one might spark the right idea.
In team settings, ask someone from a completely different domain to look at the problem.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Believing that creativity is a fixed trait rather than a skill of breaking functional fixedness.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A hiker’s water bottle breaks. He panics about dehydration for hours before realizing his plastic bag from lunch can hold water. The bag was classified as “trash,” not “container,” in his mind.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: The only difference between junk and a tool is the function your brain assigns. Break the label, and the world fills with new solutions.
